name: Real-time KV / in-memory state
parent_research_topic: Beava's current market position — competitor archetypes and market segments beava is positioned in or against, evaluated against the use-case map in ../beava-use-cases/

competitive_landscape.incumbents: The real-time KV / in-memory-state segment is the densest and most contested of any beava-adjacent market, and 2025-2026 reshaped it more than any year since Redis itself shipped in 2009. Five archetypes matter: (A) Valkey — the Linux-Foundation-stewarded BSD-3-clause fork of Redis 7.2.4 that became the cloud default in 2025-2026 (AWS ElastiCache for Valkey is the default ElastiCache engine, GCP Memorystore for Valkey ships as a separate first-class service, Ubuntu 26.04 ships Valkey as the `redis` package); Valkey 8.1 publishes ~8% higher ops/sec, 22% lower p99, and 20% lower memory than Redis OSS 7.2. (B) Redis 8 — relicensed in May 2025 by antirez under a tri-license (AGPLv3 + RSALv2 + SSPLv1) after the March 2024 SSPL/RSALv2 controversy; Redis 8 GA folded JSON, time-series, the five probabilistic structures (Bloom, Cuckoo, Count-Min-Sketch, Top-K, t-digest) and Vector Sets (HNSW, beta) into core, but RedisGears triggers/functions (TFCALL/TFUNCTION) were deprecated and will be removed. (C) Dragonfly — multi-threaded shared-nothing Redis-protocol server publishing ~2.4x throughput vs Valkey on 16 vCPUs and ~4.5x on 48 vCPUs on GCP, with 38% less memory; BSL-licensed (source-available, not OSI). (D) Aerospike — the high-end commercial flash+RAM hybrid KV that owns the tier-1 AdTech and fraud feature-store accounts (Trade Desk, Criteo, PayPal, Barclays, LexisNexis, Sony Interactive Entertainment, Quantcast, Adobe, Airtel, HDFC, Grab, TransUnion, Wayfair); proprietary commercial. (E) Hazelcast (JVM in-memory data grid, ~10M events/sec/node, stream processing built-in, Apache-2.0 community + Hazelcast Enterprise commercial) and RonDB (the world's-fastest-KV claim, ~100M lookups/sec via REST, GPLv2, exclusive online-store backing for Hopsworks Feature Store) and KeyDB (multi-threaded Redis fork, now under Snap, less active in 2025-2026). Adjacent generic/feature-store competitors that consume this layer: Tecton (acquired by Databricks 2025), Feast (Linux Foundation, Redis/DynamoDB backed), Chalk, Fennel (acquired by Databricks April 2025), Featureform (acquired by Redis October 2025, launched as Redis Feature Form in preview April 2026), Hopsworks (RonDB-backed), SageMaker Feature Store (DynamoDB-backed), Vertex AI Feature Store (Bigtable-backed). Materialize / RisingWave / Flink / Spark Real-Time Mode occupy the streaming-compute lane above the KV.
competitive_landscape.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Per beava's stated use-case footprint, the named incumbents are: (Use 3 — AdTech frequency capping & pacing) Aerospike is the overwhelming default (Trade Desk, Criteo, MGID, fuboTV publicly named); Redis Enterprise + Lua is the broad mid-market default (AWS Architecture Blog 'Serving Billions of Ads in Just 100ms Using Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS)'); SpringServe / FreeWheel / Kevel bundle capping at the ad-server layer. (Use 12 — dynamic pricing / surge) Redis + Lua for hot demand counters; Aerospike + ScyllaDB / DynamoDB for the online tier under Tecton (DoorDash flagship), Hopsworks (Clicklease), Chalk (Whatnot 300M features/sec), Fennel (Databricks-acquired April 2025); Materialize / RisingWave / ksqlDB for SQL-on-streams (Riskified). (Use 14b — usage-based billing / metering) Stripe Billing Meter Events / Meter Event Streams v2 (post-Metronome-acquisition January 2026), Lago (Apache-2.0 OSS, 1M EPS on ClickHouse Cloud), OpenMeter (YC-backed Apache-2.0), Orb (250k+ EPS SQL-over-raw-events), Cloudflare Durable Objects, Redis-Lua for the inline-quota-gate, Aerospike at the high end. (Use 18a — online FS for fraud) Tecton (Coinbase, Plaid Signal), Hopsworks (RonDB-backed SIGMOD 2024 paper, 10x lower p99 vs SageMaker/Vertex, 1.93ms avg / 3ms p99 100-row batches), Chalk, Fennel, Feast + Redis, Aerospike (PayPal 1M TPS, JPMorgan Chase 9ms p99, Barclays, LexisNexis 130M daily txns, Criteo 78% hardware reduction vs Couchbase+Memcached), Redis Feature Form (Redis-acquired-Featureform, April 2026 preview). (Use 18b — online FS for recsys/ranking) DoorDash on ElastiCache (>20M feature reads/sec, ~1000 lookups per prediction), Whatnot on Chalk (300M features/sec), Pinterest Manas/TransAct V2, Sony PlayStation on Aerospike, Swiggy ElastiCache 50M QPS, Myntra Aerospike, Tecton (Coinbase sequence features), Fennel (Upwork, Cricut), Metarank (open-source learn-to-rank, Redis-backed).
competitive_landscape.oss_license_posture: Mixed but the segment has hardened around permissive-or-fork posture in 2025-2026. Valkey: BSD-3-clause, Linux Foundation governance. Redis 8: tri-licensed AGPLv3 (since May 2025) + RSALv2 (source-available) + SSPLv1 — the AGPLv3 option is OSI-approved but its copyleft scope blocks many enterprise procurement filters, and the original 2024 'rug-pull' to SSPL/RSALv2 burned community trust. Dragonfly: BSL (source-available, not OSI). Aerospike: proprietary commercial (with a Community Edition under AGPL). Hazelcast: Apache-2.0 community + Hazelcast Enterprise. RonDB: GPLv2. KeyDB: BSD-3-clause (under Snap). Beava: Apache-2.0 — strictly more permissive than every named incumbent except Valkey (BSD ≈ Apache), and far more permissive than Redis 8 / Dragonfly / Aerospike / RonDB. The Redis-Valkey split being resolved in Valkey's favor at the hyperscalers means license posture is now a hard buyer filter, not a tiebreaker — beava's Apache-2.0 is a real (but no longer uniquely-differentiating, since Valkey is also OSS) wedge.
competitive_landscape.hyperscaler_bundling_threat: High. This is the single highest-bundling-threat segment in the beava use-case map. Every hyperscaler now ships a managed in-memory KV at a price-point and operational footprint a single-binary OSS challenger must beat: AWS ElastiCache for Valkey (20% cheaper than Redis SKU, drop-in compatible, default for new AWS deployments), AWS MemoryDB for Valkey (durable variant), GCP Memorystore for Valkey ($0.034/GB-hour Standard vs $0.0425 Redis), Azure Cache for Redis (Azure leans Redis-licensed). On top of that, Redis Feature Form (launched April 2026, preview) is the explicit bundling threat against Beava in the feature-store role: it folds Featureform's batch+stream pipeline, multi-tenancy, and RBAC into Redis Cloud, which any team already on Redis Cloud gets effectively bundled. Databricks bundling Tecton (acquired 2025) + Fennel (acquired April 2025) into the Lakebase/Feature Serving offering is the equivalent bundling-threat one layer up. The 'good enough' alternative for >80% of beava-relevant workloads is now Valkey-on-ElastiCache + a thin aggregation script — single-binary OSS challengers compete on (a) latency under 1ms TCP (where Valkey/Redis are 1-5ms on Lua paths), (b) declarative aggregation primitives (where Valkey/Redis require Lua or RedisTimeSeries downsampling), (c) WAL-grade per-entity durability (where Redis AOF is per-instance not per-entity).
competitive_landscape.integration_surface: Buyers in this segment expect a mix of: (i) Kafka / Kinesis / Pulsar producers — the default for Feast, Tecton, Hopsworks, Chalk, Fennel, OpenMeter, Lago integration paths, and the assumption baked into AWS RTB Fabric reference architectures. Beava does NOT ship a native Kafka consumer in v0 — a documented sidecar pattern (a thin Go/Rust Kafka-to-beava-push process) is the standard workaround across the use cases, and the absence is the most frequently-cited gap from the use-case research. (ii) Direct HTTP webhook / mobile-SDK push — common for adtech win-notice callbacks, billing meter events, marketplace clickstreams; beava's HTTP/JSON :8080 fits cleanly. (iii) Framed TCP+msgpack — beava's :8081, novel to the segment, and the source of its sub-ms latency edge over Redis (Redis RESP is text-framed; Valkey 8.1 adds I/O offload but the wire is unchanged). (iv) gRPC — not natively supported by beava; required for some banking/fintech procurement evaluations. (v) Spark Real-Time Mode / Flink sinks pushing pre-aggregated features — the Feast/Tecton 'materialise offline, write to online' pattern; beava has no documented bulk-load API for warehouse-computed feature sets. (vi) CloudEvents — emerging standard, especially for billing metering (OpenMeter pattern); not native to beava. Net: beava's push-on-event surface is the right shape for application-direct-push and webhook patterns but is at a friction-point for Kafka-first and warehouse-materialisation-first buyer cohorts who dominate the named Tecton/Feast/Hopsworks accounts.
competitive_landscape.scoring_engine_coupling: Both, by design — KV is the substrate. Frequency capping (Use 3) and quota gates (Use 14b) are deterministic rules read directly from the KV. Pricing (Use 12), fraud scoring (Use 18a), and recsys ranking (Use 18b) layer an ML scorer (XGBoost / LightGBM / DLRM / two-tower / cross-encoder / transformer) above the KV, with the KV serving 20-500 features per decision via batched reads. Pacing controllers (Use 3, Use 12) layer a separate control-loop service on top. Beava sits below all three patterns and exposes the same batch_get primitive to each — the scoring engine is decoupled and beava neither chooses it nor competes with it.

beava_position_lens.beava_credible_wedge: Five wedges that hold up against the 2025-2026 incumbent set: (1) Sub-millisecond TCP+msgpack get/batch_get vs Redis-Lua 1-5ms and Vertex AI Feature Store ~30ms — beava's wire format and threading model put it in Aerospike/Dragonfly latency territory on commodity hardware, with the published 684k EPS sustained on a single Apple-M4 core as the headline. (2) ~50-60 first-class aggregation primitives baked into the server vs Redis/Valkey requiring Lua scripts or RedisGears (the latter deprecated in 2025) or RedisTimeSeries downsampling — the 'windowed counters, velocities, distributions, recencies, n_unique sketches' shape that Tecton/Hopsworks/Chalk/Feast push to Flink/Spark upstream of the KV is collapsed into beava's @bv.table. This is the single most defensible differentiator against the Redis/Valkey-as-feature-store pattern. (3) Single binary, no Kafka/Flink/Redis-cluster dependency — beava ships as one Rust process with WAL; the (Kafka + Flink + Redis + Feast) or (Tecton managed) two-or-more-box norm is a hard sell for mid-market teams without a streaming-platform team. The Lago/OpenMeter pattern (ClickHouse + Kafka + custom Go consumer) is also collapsed. (4) Apache-2.0 with no open-core split and no SSPL/BSL trap — strictly more permissive than Redis 8 (AGPLv3/RSALv2/SSPLv1 tri-license), Dragonfly (BSL), Aerospike Enterprise (commercial), RonDB (GPLv2), Hazelcast Enterprise; comparable to Valkey (BSD-3) and Lago (Apache-2.0). (5) WAL+snapshot per-entity durability with refuse-on-network-FS invariant — Redis AOF is per-instance and cannot give the 'fsync this counter, not the whole store' semantic that billing metering (Use 14b) and exact fraud counters (Use 18a) need; Aerospike has hybrid memory/SSD but at a license cost; beava's WAL is the right shape, conceptually equivalent to Aerospike's persistence guarantees at the per-key level without the commercial license.
beava_position_lens.beava_disqualifiers: Concrete gaps that block production adoption in this segment today, in rough order of pain (sourced from the underlying use-case research): (1) No TLS / no auth on :8080 / :8081 / :8090 — disqualifying for every production deployment outside a tightly controlled VPC; every named managed competitor (Valkey-on-ElastiCache, Redis Enterprise, Aerospike, Hazelcast, Tecton, Hopsworks, SageMaker FS, Vertex AI FS, Redis Feature Form) ships TLS + IAM out of the box. This is the single highest-priority gap. (2) No in-process sharding / consistent hashing — single-binary v0 caps at roughly 684k EPS and a single box's worth of RAM, fine for mid-market but 10-100x short of tier-1 DSP / exchange / global bank scale; Aerospike's 20-node petabyte-scale Criteo benchmark and PayPal's 1M TPS sit beyond a single beava box. (3) No multi-region active-active replication — frequency caps, fraud counters, and credit-balance wallets for global tenants need consistent counters across regions; Aerospike XDR, Hazelcast WAN replication, and Valkey 9.0 cluster bus are the explicit incumbent features. (4) No native idempotency-key dedup on the wire — every billing-metering, ad-tech-cap-counter, and fraud-counter use case requires 'increment-once-per-event-id-within-window'; Stripe pattern is 24h dedup, OpenMeter is 32d. (5) No triggers / 'fire callback when counter crosses threshold' — Use 3 (pacing), Use 12 (auto-markdown/auto-reorder/auto-surge), Use 14b (credit-balance 50/80/95/100% alerts and kill-switch), Use 18a (rate-limit-a-BIN, freeze-account) all want this; RedisGears triggers being deprecated in 2025 leaves a gap on the Redis side, but Aerospike UDFs and Hazelcast Jet listeners cover it. (6) No multi-tenancy / namespace ACLs — required for SaaS feature-platform hosting, managed bidder/SSP serving multiple DSPs, billing platforms serving multiple tenants, hotel-RM SaaS serving thousands of properties. (7) No Kafka consumer entrypoint — the dominant ingest pattern in the segment; a documented sidecar is the workaround but absence is friction at every named Tecton/Feast/Hopsworks/Chalk/Fennel buyer cohort. (8) No point-in-time-correct offline materialisation — the headline 'training-serving parity' feature Tecton/Hopsworks/Chalk/Fennel/Featureform market against the Redis+Lua DIY pattern. (9) No bulk-load / warehouse-sink API — beava expects per-event push, not 'load this Parquet file' from a nightly Spark job. (10) No ANN / vector primitive — Redis 8 ships Vector Sets (HNSW) in beta, Aerospike has Vector Search; beava is feature-serving, not candidate-retrieval, but for the recsys-FS-role buyer (Use 18b) this is an integration gap. (11) Cold-start WAL replay time on 100+ GB hot state is unbenchmarked publicly. (12) No managed/hosted offering — competitors at this scale all have a managed tier; beava buyers must operate the box themselves. (13) Limited public case studies in this exact segment — Aerospike has Trade Desk + Criteo + PayPal on the record; Valkey has Snap and growing AWS reference customers; Redis Feature Form will land April 2026 with Featureform's existing references; beava has none.

evidence_and_verdict.validation_signals_today: Repo evidence (strong on primitives, weaker on go-to-market): beava ships ~60 aggregation primitives in python/beava/_agg.py and demonstrated workload configs in crates/beava-bench/configs/ (fraud-team.json, large-with-sketches.json, geo.json), runnable demos in python/beava/demos/{adtech,ecommerce,fraud}, and the published 684k EPS single-core TCP+msgpack benchmark. The adtech demo events.jsonl already keys (user_id, campaign_id) — exactly the frequency-cap shape — making a 1-afternoon proof-of-concept demo feasible. NO dedicated dynamic-pricing, metering, online-FS-for-fraud-classifier, or recsys-rerank demo exists in /python/beava/demos/ as of the snapshot. NO public production users or named case studies in the real-time-KV segment have been identified — every use-case dossier reports 'no public beava users in this domain yet [uncertain]'. Public GitHub stars / forks / Discord activity for beava itself are below the threshold where they show up in 2025-2026 industry reporting alongside Valkey (Linux Foundation cohort), Dragonfly (~26k stars), Lago (tens of thousands), OpenMeter (YC-backed cohort). Adjacent comparable references that validate the segment shape (not beava): DoorDash 20M feature reads/sec on ElastiCache, Criteo 290M QPS / 78% hardware reduction on Aerospike, PayPal 1M TPS on Aerospike, JPMorgan 9ms p99 on Inferentia3+feature-fetch, Whatnot 300M features/sec on Chalk, Pinterest Manas 1.2M user-action events/sec, Tecton 0.8ms published feature retrieval, Hopsworks 1.93ms avg / 3ms p99 100-row batches, Stripe Billing 10k req/s livemode default rate-limit, Lago 1M EPS on ClickHouse, AWS RTB Fabric reference architecture on Aerospike + ElastiCache. The contrast is stark: every named competitor has at least one tier-1 public reference; beava has none in this segment.
evidence_and_verdict.verdict: Compete — beava has a genuine wedge (declarative aggregation primitives + single binary + sub-ms TCP + Apache-2.0) against the Redis+Lua DIY pattern that dominates mid-market AdTech, fraud, recsys, and billing-metering, but tier-1 wins (Trade Desk-class AdTech, PayPal-class fraud, DoorDash-class recsys, global metering) require closing the TLS/auth + sharding + replication + idempotency-key gaps over 6-12 months. Lead-tier positioning is possible against (Redis+Lua) and (Lago/OpenMeter ClickHouse) in mid-market accounts; Compete-tier against (Tecton/Hopsworks/Chalk/Fennel managed feature stores); Watch-tier against (Aerospike at tier-1 scale, Redis Feature Form once GA, hyperscaler bundles).
